name: Norovirus (winter vomiting bug)
definition: A highly contagious viral infection of the gut that causes sudden vomiting and diarrhoea.
overview: Norovirus is a very contagious stomach bug that causes vomiting and diarrhoea. In the UK it often circulates in winter, though it can occur at any time of year. Most people recover within a few days without specific treatment. Young children, older adults and people with other illnesses are at higher risk of dehydration.
causes: Infection with norovirus, which spreads mainly by the faecal-oral route.
Direct contact with an infected person.
Eating or drinking contaminated food or water.
Raw shellfish, especially oysters, which concentrate virus particles from contaminated water.
Food handled by an infected food worker, particularly ready-to-eat cold foods such as salads and sandwiches.
riskFactors: Very young or older age, or other illness, which raise the risk of dehydration.
A weakened immune system, which raises the risk of dehydration.
Staying in hospitals or long-term care facilities, where outbreaks are commonly reported.
Close living quarters such as cruise ships, camps and dormitories.
signs: A high temperature in some people.
Signs of dehydration, such as dark urine, passing less urine than usual, or fewer wet nappies in babies.
complications: Dehydration, which is the main complication.
Severe dehydration, which may need intravenous fluids.
Hospital treatment for some people, usually the very young or very old.
diagnosis: Diagnosis is usually based on the symptoms. Laboratory testing of stool is mainly used to identify clusters of illness during outbreak investigations.
treatment: There is no specific cure or antiviral medicine, and antibiotics do not work because the cause is a virus. Care focuses on rest and drinking plenty of fluids to prevent dehydration. Oral rehydration solutions from a pharmacy are used when there are signs of dehydration, and severe cases may need intravenous fluids.
prevention: Washing hands with soap and water is the key measure, because alcohol-based hand gels do not inactivate the virus. UK guidance advises staying away from work, school and hospital or care home visits, and avoiding preparing food for others, until 48 hours after symptoms stop. The CDC says no norovirus vaccine is currently available.
seekCare: Call 999 or go to A&E for blood in vomit, green vomit in an adult, a severe headache or difficulty breathing, or for serious dehydration signs such as unusual sleepiness, dizziness on standing, or fast breathing or heart rate. NHS 111 is the route if diarrhoea lasts more than 7 days, vomiting lasts more than 2 days, fluids cannot be kept down, there is blood in the diarrhoea, or a baby or young child shows signs of dehydration. A pharmacist can advise on oral rehydration, and UKHSA asks people with symptoms to phone a GP or NHS 111 rather than attend A&E or a surgery unless advised.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of norovirus?
sections.body:
The NHS says the main symptoms of norovirus usually start suddenly. They are feeling sick, vomiting and diarrhoea. Some people also have a high temperature, a headache, tummy pain or body aches.

The CDC says symptoms typically begin 12 to 48 hours after exposure. Most people get better within one to three days, and the NHS says most feel better within about two days. UKHSA describes most people as recovering in two to three days without needing any medicine.

Vomiting and diarrhoea make the body lose water and salts, which is why dehydration is the main concern. Signs described by the NHS include dark urine and passing less urine than usual. In babies and young children, signs include few or no tears when crying and fewer wet nappies.

sections.heading: How does norovirus spread?
sections.body:
The CDC says norovirus spreads mainly by the faecal-oral route, either from person to person or through contaminated food or water. It can also spread through contaminated surfaces. The CDC says as few as 18 virus particles may be enough to cause infection.

UKHSA says people are most infectious while they have symptoms but can also pass the virus on before symptoms start and after they stop. The CDC says people can spread it for up to 72 hours after recovering, and in some cases for two weeks or more.

Raw shellfish, especially oysters, are a frequent source of infection, because filter-feeding shellfish concentrate virus particles from contaminated water. Food prepared by a sick worker is another route, and contaminated ready-to-eat cold foods such as salads and sandwiches are a particular risk. The CDC says hospitals, long-term care facilities, cruise ships, camps, dormitories and hotels are frequent places for outbreaks.

sections.heading: How is norovirus diagnosed and treated?
sections.body:
The CDC Yellow Book says diagnosis is usually based on symptoms. Laboratory testing is used mainly to identify clusters of illness during outbreak investigations. When testing is done, a PCR test can detect the virus in stool samples.

There is no specific treatment for norovirus, and antibiotics do not work because it is caused by a virus. Care centres on resting and drinking plenty of fluids to prevent dehydration. The NHS advises against fruit juice and fizzy drinks, which can make diarrhoea worse. It also advises against aspirin for children under 16.

For babies, the NHS describes continuing breast or formula feeds in small, frequent amounts, with formula made up at its usual strength. A pharmacist can supply oral rehydration powder when there are signs of dehydration. The CDC says oral rehydration fluids help in mild cases, while severe cases may need intravenous fluids.

sections.heading: When should someone get help for the vomiting bug?
sections.body:
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for blood in vomit, green vomit in an adult, a severe headache or difficulty breathing. The NHS dehydration page lists unusual sleepiness, dizziness on standing, and fast breathing or heart rate as signs of serious dehydration needing urgent treatment.

The NHS says to call NHS 111 if diarrhoea lasts more than 7 days or vomiting lasts more than 2 days. NHS 111 is also the route for a worry about a baby under 12 months, a baby or child who stops feeding, someone who cannot keep fluids down, or blood in the diarrhoea. A child under 5 with signs of dehydration, such as fewer wet nappies, is also advised to get NHS 111 advice.

UKHSA asks people with symptoms not to go to A&E or a GP surgery unless a healthcare professional advises it. A phone call to the GP or NHS 111 is the suggested first step, and a pharmacist can advise on oral rehydration.

sections.heading: How can the spread of norovirus be reduced?
sections.body:
Washing hands with soap and water is the main measure. Alcohol-based hand gels do not kill norovirus. The NHS says clothes and bedding soiled with vomit or faeces should be washed hot, and surfaces cleaned promptly.

UKHSA advises staying at home until 48 hours after symptoms stop, and avoiding preparing food for others for the same time. The NHS and UKHSA also ask people who are unwell to keep away from hospitals and care homes.

In care homes and hospitals, UKHSA-linked guidance describes isolating affected residents in their own room, enhanced cleaning, and closing affected areas to new admissions. The CDC says no vaccine or antiviral is currently available. It adds that at least two vaccines were in clinical trials as of April 2025.

faqs.q: Can you catch norovirus more than once?
faqs.a: The CDC describes immunity to norovirus as short-lived. It says protection against the same strain lasts between 6 months and 2 years. The CDC also says no norovirus vaccine or antiviral is currently available. Because no vaccine exists, hygiene measures remain the main way to reduce spread.

faqs.q: Do antibiotics help with the vomiting bug?
faqs.a: UKHSA says antibiotics do not work on norovirus because it is a virus. There is no specific treatment. Care focuses on rest and drinking plenty of fluids to replace the water and salts lost through vomiting and diarrhoea. A pharmacist can supply oral rehydration powder if there are signs of dehydration.

UKHSA says people are most infectious when they have symptoms, but can spread the virus before symptoms start and after they stop. UK advice is to stay at home, and avoid preparing food for others, until 48 hours after symptoms have stopped. The CDC says people can shed the virus for up to 72 hours after recovery, and in some cases for two weeks or more.

faqs.q: Do alcohol hand gels kill norovirus?
faqs.a: The NHS and the CDC both say alcohol-based hand gels do not kill norovirus. Handwashing with soap and water is the recommended measure, especially after using the toilet and before handling food. Soiled surfaces also need cleaning, as the virus spreads through surfaces as well as by direct contact.

faqs.q: Why do outbreaks happen in hospitals and care homes?
faqs.a: The CDC says institutional settings such as hospitals and long-term care facilities commonly report norovirus outbreaks. The CDC also says hospital patients who are very old, very young or very ill are most harmed. For this reason, UKHSA asks people who are unwell not to visit hospitals or care homes. Outbreak measures include isolating affected residents and enhanced cleaning.
